extraction_text: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma about the superiority between householder duties and renunciation.
Bhishma explains both paths are meritorious and difficult, then recounts an ancient dialogue between Kapila and a cow.
King Uparichara prepares to sacrifice a cow to serve Tvashtri according to ancient scriptures.
Kapila, a disciplined ascetic, sees the bound cow and questions the state of truth and the Vedas.
Sage Shumarashmi enters the cow's body and questions Kapila about the validity of non-Vedic doctrines versus Vedic actions.
Kapila responds that he does not criticize the Vedas and acknowledges all life stages lead to the same goal, questioning if non-violence is superior to action.
Sage Shumarashmi argues that scriptures prescribe sacrifices for heavenly rewards, with all life forms interdependent and meant for rituals.
The text describes the essential components and philosophy of Vedic sacrifice (yajna).

attributes.action: Listing the components of a sacrifice (12 items: herbs, cattle, trees, etc., plus the Vedas, the sacrificer, and the householder's fire, totaling 17 limbs).
attributes.relationships: Establishes that sacrifice is the foundation of everything and connects the worlds.
attributes.supernatural_elements: Mentions that sacrifice leads to heaven and that 'Om' is the womb of Brahman.

extraction_text: The text explains the purpose and proper attitude for performing sacrifice.

attributes.action: Describes that one should perform sacrifice because it is right, without greed for results, without harming beings, and without hostility.
attributes.relationships: Links the sacrificer to the cosmic order through ritual.
attributes.supernatural_elements: States that proper performance of rituals with mantras (Om, Namah, Svaha, etc.) removes fear of the afterlife across the three worlds.

extraction_text: The text presents the consequences of performing and not performing sacrifice.

attributes.action: Asserts that performing sacrifice according to heavenly rules grants the great fruit of ascending to heaven after death.
attributes.relationships: Contrasts the fate of the sacrificer with the non-sacrificer.
attributes.supernatural_elements: Declares that one who does not perform sacrifice belongs neither to this world nor the other.

extraction_text: The text concludes by citing its source.

attributes.action: Identifies the passage as Chapter 260 of the Shanti Parva (Book of Peace) in the Mahabharata.
